Happy to share that this past weekend, I worked with Praniil Nagaraj to win the ElevenLabs track at RocketHacks 2026, hosted by MLH and the University of Toledo. Lots of learnings from this one: 1. Don’t rush the beginning We dove straight into building without thinking enough about structure — file organization, data flow, and how components would connect. That led to avoidable friction later. A bit more upfront planning would have saved us a lot of time. 2. Less is sometimes more We tried to pack in too many features early on. There’s a hard limit to what you can realistically build in 24 hours. Things got much smoother once we focused on a few core problems and built around those. 3. Think beyond the product During judging, we were asked about the business model — and we didn’t have a great answer. It’s easy to focus purely on building, but viability matters too. Every project needs a story for how they sustain itself. 4. Integration is always harder than expected Individual pieces worked, but connecting everything together took longer than anticipated. Save some time to get things talking to each other. Definitely one of the most intense (and rewarding) builds I’ve done, can't wait for the next one.

I'm excited to share that I recently placed Top 5 at the inaugural University of Michigan - Stephen M. Ross School of Business x University of Michigan College of Engineering AI Hackathon with Ayush Madhav Kumar , Caleb Kosel , and Sajiv Jampani . We asked a simple question: Shouldn't exam feedback reflect concept mastery instead of just question accuracy? Our solution was an AI-powered, professor-side exam analyzer that turns question-level performance into concept-based competency scores. Given any question, our tool evaluates a student's understanding of: - The core concept being tested - The foundational concepts that may influence their understanding - Any downstream concepts that could be impacted by a gap in understanding It then compiles these insights into structured class/individual level reports that professors can use to gain insights into their class's understanding of the content and provide better, targeted feedback to students. As my first hackathon, this experience was especially impactful. Beyond my first time using the technical skills involved in the project, it challenged me to think critically about potential issues and possible solutions in the educational world. I'm grateful for the team and the experience. Time to carry this momentum forward.

Vestris (YC S26) runs the entire real estate closing process. Title insurance is the thorn in the side of every home purchase in America, and almost nobody who buys it can tell you what it does. Behind the scenes, someone is opening emails one at a time as files and paperwork crawl through, manually copying info from pieces of paper. The "modern" software is a decade-old database most small shops can't even afford. So founders Aahil Valliani and Joshua Tang spent months working inside mom-and-pop title shops, closing real files alongside the processors, and built Vestris. It reads every document the moment it lands, pulls county records, drafts the title commitment, and reconciles the closing disclosure. Nothing goes out without a human signing off. Processors are handed a file with the busywork already done, so they can spend their time making judgment calls and the work clients actually remember: walking someone through the biggest purchase of their life. Vestris is already running alongside a shop settling millions in deals a month. Learn more at vestris.ai or reach out at founders@vestris.ai . Congrats on the launch, Aahil and Joshua! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gsMjiUm4

And with that my first DEFCON comes to a close. It was an absolute blast meeting new friends and visiting the villages they had there! The people here were so welcoming and kind, perfect for my first time. I will say you will meet some people that will absolutely surprise you. A key piece of advice I'll give is to see if you can find any colleagues of some of your professors. You'll get some wild stories, learn something new and have a great time! For example, I met one of the cofounders of Tor and he told me how part of Tor's infrastructure is at my university plus he knows the faculty advisor for our cybersecurity club, Prof. Ensafi. I also met some of Prof. Halderman's colleagues at the Voting Village. I'm glad I went to DEFCON before I graduate this upcoming school year. See you all next year! Hopefully, I'll be handed another free OWASP t-shirt while writing my post.(yes this did actually happen)

Over the past few days I had a blast attending Capital One’s July Tech Summit! It was great meeting other students and Capital One associates while learning more about the engineering culture and Tech Internship Program. One thing I hadn’t fully understood before was Capital One’s culture of continuous learning. From their internal colleges, to internal ML slack channels where employees share what they're learning about the field, there are endless opportunities to learn and build community. During one fun activity within the event, we were each given 10 minutes to build a “catch the cash” game. My ATTC took some creative liberty and brought the idea a little closer to home catching Dave’s Hot Chicken fries. Try to beat my high score through the link in the comments. A huge thank you to Deshae Coleman for coordinating such an engaging event and to Terris Johnson for extending this opportunity to me.
